summary:
Ulyanovsk Oblast stands under the Russian national framework, which applies in full and offers no regional deviation material enough to score separately. Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. For a visitor this means an identity document carrying an outdated marker cannot be corrected before or during travel, so any police, hotel or transport identity check reads a mismatch.

The 2013 'gay propaganda' law carries administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. The expanded statute reaches public expression that 'justifies' gender transition, and foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, detention and deportation.

Since the November 2023 Supreme Court 'extremist' designation of the international LGBT+ movement, participation carries 2 to 6 years and organising 6 to 10 years' imprisonment under Article 282.2. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 'extremism'-related convictions, about 98 administrative and 3 criminal, for alleged participation in the designated movement or displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025; between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, and 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The federal framework has been enforced inside Ulyanovsk Oblast itself. Citing an October 2024 OVD-Info report, the UK Home Office records that Ilya Zhuravlev, former head of the dialysis centre in Inza in the Ulyanovsk region, was detained in August 2024 on charges of participating in the activities of the 'extremist' 'LGBT movement' (Part 2 of Article 282.2) and coercion of a person to a sexual act (Part 1 of Article 133). Human Rights Watch separately reports that in March 2025 a Ulyanovsk-region doctor facing a maximum of one year's imprisonment for alleged sexual coercion was also prosecuted for 'involving' another man in the 'LGBT movement' and received a three-year sentence.

The UK Home Office note records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that openly LGBT+ people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to provide protection. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement has escalated in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines under those statutes bringing more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. Physical coercion against transgender people is separately documented: BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping.
localsOnly:
The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia (SOGI, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Residents of Ulyanovsk Oblast face the same document regime as all Russian citizens: gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare has been unavailable since the 2023 ban, so legal transition is closed off domestically.
outOfScopeNotes: The inventory does not resolve whether Ulyanovsk Oblast has issued any regional bylaw on 'propaganda' distinct from the federal statute, or whether local enforcement practice differs in frequency from the national average; only two federal-level enforcement actions inside the region are sourced. The outcome of the Zhuravlev and the March 2025 doctor prosecutions beyond the sentences stated is not sourced here.
